bioprocess-001.question: When the rate of an enzyme reaction follows the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax·S/(Km + S), which is the correct meaning of the Michaelis constant Km (S is the substrate concentration)?
choices: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half the maximum rate Vmax
The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate just reaches the maximum rate Vmax
A constant expressing the affinity of the enzyme for the substrate, which is larger the higher the affinity
bioprocess-001.explanation: Substituting S = Km into the equation gives v = Vmax·Km/(2Km) = Vmax/2, so Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half the maximum, and it has units of concentration (mol/L and so on). As S increases, v only approaches Vmax asymptotically and never “reaches” it at a finite concentration, so the choice defining Km as the concentration at which Vmax is reached is wrong. An enzyme with a smaller Km reaches high rates at lower substrate concentrations, so Km is smaller the higher the affinity; the choice saying it is larger for higher affinity has the direction backwards. Km equals the dissociation constant only when formation and dissociation of the enzyme–substrate complex are much faster than its breakdown into product.

bioprocess-002.question: For an enzyme reaction following the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax·S/(Km + S), which correctly describes the behavior of the reaction rate where the substrate concentration S is much smaller than Km?
choices: v is nearly constant at Vmax and can be treated as zero order in substrate concentration
v is approximately (Vmax/Km)·S and can be treated as first order in substrate concentration
v is roughly proportional to the square of the substrate concentration and can be treated as second order in substrate concentration
bioprocess-002.explanation: When S ≪ Km, the denominator Km + S is nearly equal to Km, so v ≈ (Vmax/Km)·S, a first-order reaction proportional to substrate concentration. Conversely, when S ≫ Km, the denominator is nearly equal to S, so v ≈ Vmax, a zero-order reaction independent of substrate concentration. The choice of a nearly constant Vmax (zero order) describes this high-concentration behavior, confused with the low-concentration side. The Michaelis–Menten equation never increases faster than the first power of S, so there is no region where it can be treated as second order. A characteristic of the equation is that a single expression shifts from first order to zero order depending on the concentration range.

bioprocess-003.question: Measurements of an enzyme reaction plotted as a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v on the vertical axis, 1/S on the horizontal axis) give the straight line 1/v = 0.40·(1/S) + 0.10. v is in mmol/(L·min) and S in mmol/L. What is the Michaelis constant Km?
choices: 0.25 mmol/L
0.40 mmol/L
4.0 mmol/L
bioprocess-003.explanation: Taking the reciprocal of the Michaelis–Menten equation gives 1/v = (Km/Vmax)·(1/S) + 1/Vmax, so the vertical intercept is 1/Vmax and the slope is Km/Vmax. From the intercept of 0.10, Vmax = 1/0.10 = 10 mmol/(L·min), and from the slope, Km = 0.40 × 10 = 4.0 mmol/L. 0.25 mmol/L takes the absolute value of the horizontal intercept, −1/Km, directly as Km; Km is its reciprocal. 0.40 mmol/L mistakes the slope for Km, but the slope includes Vmax. This plot is easy to read as a straight line, but note that it greatly magnifies the errors of measurements at low concentrations.

bioprocess-004.question: When a fixed concentration of a competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction, which correctly describes the change in the Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v on the vertical axis, 1/S on the horizontal axis)?
choices: The vertical intercept is unchanged and the slope increases
The slope is unchanged and only the vertical intercept increases
The horizontal intercept is unchanged and the vertical intercept increases
bioprocess-004.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the same active site, so at a sufficiently high substrate concentration the inhibition is overcome and the maximum rate Vmax does not change. On the other hand, more substrate is needed for the same rate, and the apparent Km increases to Km(1 + I/Ki). The vertical intercept 1/Vmax therefore stays the same while the slope Km/Vmax increases, and the lines with and without inhibitor cross on the vertical axis. The choice with the horizontal intercept unchanged is the pattern of noncompetitive inhibition, in which Km is unchanged and Vmax falls, with the lines crossing on the horizontal axis. The choice with the slope unchanged, a parallel shift, is the change seen in uncompetitive inhibition.

bioprocess-005.question: In batch culture of microorganisms, which is correct about the change with time of the cell concentration X in the exponential growth phase (specific growth rate μ = (1/X)(dX/dt))?
choices: X increases linearly in proportion to time, and the slope is the specific growth rate μ
Plotting ln X against time gives a straight line whose slope is the specific growth rate μ
Because substrate is plentiful, μ keeps increasing with time and X increases in proportion to the square of time
bioprocess-005.explanation: In the exponential growth phase substrate is plentiful and μ stays nearly constant (close to μmax in the Monod equation). Integrating dX/dt = μX gives X = X₀·exp(μt), so ln X is linear in time and μ is found from the slope of the straight line on a semilog plot. Linear growth of X in proportion to time would mean a constant growth rate dX/dt, unlike exponential growth, in which cells grow faster the more of them there are. μ is constant; it does not keep increasing. Later, when growth stops because of substrate depletion or accumulation of metabolites, the culture enters the stationary phase.

bioprocess-006.question: The specific growth rate of a microorganism in the exponential growth phase is a constant μ = 0.35 h⁻¹. Approximately how long does it take for the cell concentration to double (the doubling time)?
choices: About 0.24 h
About 2.9 h
About 2.0 h
bioprocess-006.explanation: In exponential growth X = X₀·exp(μt), the time for X to reach 2X₀ is td = ln2/μ = 0.693 ÷ 0.35 ≈ 1.98 h, or about 2.0 h. About 2.9 h takes 1/μ as the doubling time; this is the time for the cell concentration to increase e-fold (about 2.7 times). About 0.24 h multiplies ln2 by μ instead of dividing, and its units become h⁻¹, not a time. The doubling time is inversely proportional to the specific growth rate, so doubling μ halves the doubling time. Fast-growing bacteria such as E. coli can have doubling times of around 20–30 minutes under good conditions.

bioprocess-007.question: Which correctly describes fed-batch culture?
choices: Medium is fed at a constant flow rate and culture broth is withdrawn at the same flow rate, keeping the liquid volume constant
Substrate is added little by little during the culture to keep the substrate concentration in the vessel low, and no broth is withdrawn along the way, so the liquid volume increases
All the substrate needed is charged at the start of the culture, and nothing is added or withdrawn along the way
bioprocess-007.explanation: Fed-batch culture supplies substrate gradually to match the progress of the culture, and because nothing is withdrawn, the liquid volume increases with time. Keeping the substrate concentration low avoids growth inhibition by high substrate concentrations, and in baker's yeast avoids the phenomenon in which high glucose produces ethanol even under aerobic conditions and lowers the cell yield, so the culture can reach high cell concentrations. The choice that withdraws broth at the feed rate describes continuous culture with constant volume (the chemostat), and the choice that charges all the substrate at the start describes batch culture. Fed-batch culture is distinguished from continuous culture by having no withdrawal, and from batch culture by adding substrate along the way.

bioprocess-008.question: A perfectly mixed continuous culture (chemostat) is operated at a constant dilution rate D (feed flow rate ÷ broth volume). Ignoring cell death and maintenance metabolism, which is correct about the steady state?
choices: The specific growth rate μ equals the dilution rate D
The specific growth rate μ always equals the maximum specific growth rate μmax, regardless of the dilution rate
The specific growth rate μ equals the reciprocal of the dilution rate, 1/D
bioprocess-008.explanation: The cell balance is dX/dt = μX − DX, and at steady state, where growth balances washout, μ = D. In a chemostat, therefore, setting the dilution rate sets the specific growth rate. μ is set by the residual substrate concentration in the vessel through the Monod equation; lowering D lowers the substrate concentration and so lowers μ, so μ is not always μmax. 1/D is the mean residence time, with units of time, so it cannot be compared with μ, which has units of h⁻¹. Because of this property, the chemostat is also used for experiments that study physiological states at a fixed growth rate.

bioprocess-009.question: A microorganism following the Monod equation μ = μmax·S/(Ks + S) is grown in continuous culture in a chemostat. With μmax = 0.50 h⁻¹, Ks = 0.25 g/L and a feed substrate concentration S₀ = 1.0 g/L, what is the critical dilution rate at which washout begins (ignore cell death and maintenance metabolism)?
bioprocess-009.explanation: The substrate concentration in the vessel cannot exceed the feed concentration S₀, so the maximum specific growth rate the cells can achieve is μmax·S₀/(Ks + S₀) = 0.50 × 1.0 ÷ (0.25 + 1.0) = 0.40 h⁻¹. If the dilution rate exceeds this, growth cannot keep up with the outflow and the cells are washed out. 0.50 h⁻¹ is the approximation for S₀ much larger than Ks, which cannot be used here because S₀ is only four times Ks. 0.10 h⁻¹ puts Ks in the numerator by mistake. In actual operation, a dilution rate is chosen with a margin below the critical dilution rate.

bioprocess-010.question: A microorganism following the Monod equation is grown in a chemostat with μmax = 0.50 h⁻¹, Ks = 0.20 g/L, a feed substrate concentration S₀ = 10 g/L, a cell yield Yx/s = 0.50 g cells/g substrate and a dilution rate D = 0.30 h⁻¹. Ignoring cell death and maintenance metabolism, approximately what is the steady-state cell concentration (the feed medium contains no cells)?
choices: About 4.9 g/L
About 9.7 g/L
bioprocess-010.explanation: At steady state μ = D, so from the Monod equation the residual substrate concentration is S = Ks·D/(μmax − D) = 0.20 × 0.30 ÷ (0.50 − 0.30) = 0.30 g/L. The substrate consumed is S₀ − S = 9.7 g/L, and the cell concentration is X = Yx/s(S₀ − S) = 0.50 × 9.7 = 4.85 g/L, or about 4.9 g/L. 5.0 g/L treats the residual substrate as zero, an approximation that becomes worse the closer D is to the critical dilution rate. About 9.7 g/L forgets the yield and takes the substrate consumed directly as the cell mass. The cell productivity DX under these conditions is about 1.5 g/(L·h).

bioprocess-011.question: Taking cell maintenance metabolism (substrate consumed to keep cells alive even without growth) into account, how does the apparent cell yield Yx/s observed in continuous culture relate to the specific growth rate μ?
choices: The smaller μ is, the larger the share of substrate going to maintenance, so the apparent yield becomes smaller
The smaller μ is, the larger the share of substrate going to growth, so the apparent yield becomes larger
The apparent yield does not depend on μ and is a constant set only by the organism and the substrate
bioprocess-011.explanation: Dividing substrate consumption into growth and maintenance gives the Pirt equation 1/Yx/s = 1/YG + m/μ (YG is the true growth yield and m the maintenance coefficient). Maintenance consumption m is nearly independent of μ, so the more slowly the cells grow, the larger the share of total consumption that goes to maintenance, and the apparent yield falls. The choice saying the apparent yield grows as μ falls has the direction backwards. Treating the yield as constant is only an approximation valid when μ is large and m/μ is small. The equation shows that even when a high yield is wanted, lowering the dilution rate too far makes the maintenance loss noticeable.

bioprocess-012.question: In an aerated stirred tank, the oxygen transfer rate OTR = kLa(C* − CL) is to be increased (C* is the saturation dissolved oxygen concentration and CL the dissolved oxygen concentration in the liquid). Which method raises the OTR mainly by increasing C* rather than kLa?
choices: Raising the impeller speed so that the mixing itself raises the saturation dissolved-oxygen concentration
Increasing the aeration rate so that the oxygen partial pressure in the bubbles rises to several times that of air
Raising the vessel pressure or sparging oxygen-enriched air to raise the oxygen partial pressure in the gas
bioprocess-012.explanation: C* is proportional to the oxygen partial pressure in the gas phase (Henry's law), so raising the vessel pressure or using a gas with a higher oxygen concentration increases C* and enlarges the driving force C* − CL. Stronger agitation makes bubbles finer, increasing the gas–liquid interfacial area a and also raising the liquid-side mass transfer coefficient kL, so it is a way of increasing kLa. Increasing the aeration rate also increases the amount of bubbles (gas holdup) and the interfacial area, mainly raising kLa. Methods that raise kLa come with more agitation power, along with heat generation and shear effects on cells, so the methods are combined to suit the purpose.

bioprocess-013.question: In an aerobic culture, the oxygen uptake rate of the whole cell population is 360 mg-O₂/(L·h). With a saturation dissolved oxygen concentration C* = 7.0 mg/L, and the dissolved oxygen to be held at CL = 1.0 mg/L, what volumetric oxygen transfer coefficient kLa is required at steady state?
choices: 60 h⁻¹
About 51 h⁻¹
bioprocess-013.explanation: At steady state, the rate of oxygen transfer from bubbles to the liquid balances the oxygen uptake rate of the cells. From kLa(C* − CL) = 360 mg/(L·h), kLa = 360 ÷ (7.0 − 1.0) = 60 h⁻¹. About 51 h⁻¹ uses C* = 7.0 mg/L as the driving force; the driving force is smaller by the dissolved oxygen remaining in the liquid, so this would leave the culture short of oxygen. 360 h⁻¹ divides by CL alone. The higher the dissolved oxygen is held, the smaller the driving force and the larger the required kLa, so it is sensible to set it just above the minimum concentration the cells need (the critical dissolved oxygen concentration).

bioprocess-014.question: A heat-resistant spore has a D value (the time to reduce the viable count to 1/10) of 2.0 min at 121 ℃. How many minutes of heating at 121 ℃ are needed to reduce the spores in a medium from an initial 10⁶ to 10⁻³, corresponding to a survival probability (thermal death follows first-order kinetics)?
choices: 12 min
18 min
About 41 min
bioprocess-014.explanation: For first-order thermal death, log₁₀(N₀/N) = t/D. Going from 10⁶ to 10⁻³ is a reduction of nine orders of magnitude, so t = 2.0 × 9 = 18 min. 12 min is the value for six orders, taking the survivors down to one; since a single survivor causes contamination, the sterilization target is set at a survival probability far below one (here, one in a thousand). About 41 min counts the orders with the natural logarithm, ln(10⁹) ≈ 20.7, instead of the common logarithm; note that the D value is based on tenfold reductions. In real sterilization, death during heating and cooling is also integrated in the evaluation.

bioprocess-015.question: In heat sterilization of media, which correctly explains why high-temperature, short-time continuous sterilization (for example, a few seconds to a few minutes at 140 ℃) is better at limiting thermal degradation of medium components than long batch sterilization at 121 ℃?
choices: Because degradation reactions of medium components stop at high temperatures
Because thermal death of spores and degradation of medium components have the same temperature dependence, so a shorter heating time reduces both
Because the activation energy for thermal death of spores is larger than that for degradation of medium components, so raising the temperature speeds up death much more
bioprocess-015.explanation: The activation energy for thermal death of spores is large, typically about 250–350 kJ/mol, making it more sensitive to temperature than degradation of medium components such as vitamins (mostly smaller, around 100 kJ/mol or less). By the Arrhenius equation, raising the temperature from 121 ℃ to 140 ℃ speeds up a 300 kJ/mol reaction about 67 times, but a 90 kJ/mol reaction only about 3.5 times. The same killing effect is achieved in a shorter time, so less degradation occurs. Degradation reactions do not stop at high temperature; they actually speed up. If the two had the same temperature dependence, the degradation for the same killing effect would be the same at any temperature, and high-temperature, short-time sterilization would offer no advantage.

bioprocess-016.question: A spore has a D value of 1.5 min at 121 ℃. If the temperature rise needed to reduce the D value to one tenth (the z value) is 10 ℃, about what is the D value at 115 ℃?
choices: About 0.38 min
2.4 min
About 6.0 min
bioprocess-016.explanation: By definition of the z value, the D value becomes ten times larger for every drop of z in temperature, so D(T) = D(121 ℃) × 10^((121 − T)/z). At 115 ℃, 10^(6/10) = 10^0.6 ≈ 3.98, so D ≈ 1.5 × 3.98 ≈ 5.97 min, or about 6.0 min. About 0.38 min reverses the sign of the exponent, 1.5 × 10^(−0.6), which contradicts the fact that death slows as the temperature falls. 2.4 min is 1.5 × (1 + 0.6), a linear approximation of the power of ten. A drop of only 6 ℃ makes the required heating time about four times longer, so in sterilization it is important to control the temperature and to check spots that heat up slowly.

bioprocess-017.question: The product formation rate is expressed by the Luedeking–Piret equation rP = α·(dX/dt) + β·X (X is the cell concentration). Which is correct about the production of a secondary metabolite such as penicillin?
choices: It is growth-associated, dominated by the α term, so it is fastest in the exponential phase and stops as soon as growth stops
It is non-growth-associated, dominated by the β term, so it continues in proportion to cell mass after growth nearly stops
Its rate is constant (zero order) regardless of cell concentration, so it increases in proportion to time at any stage of culture
bioprocess-017.explanation: In the Luedeking–Piret equation, the α term represents formation proportional to the growth rate (growth-associated) and the β term represents formation proportional to the amount of cells (non-growth-associated). Primary metabolites tied directly to energy metabolism, such as ethanol, are dominated by the α term and are made along with growth. Secondary metabolites such as penicillin are produced mainly after growth has slowed, so the β term dominates, and operation separates a growth phase from a production phase, which is prolonged by fed-batch feeding. The choice saying production stops when growth stops describes primary metabolites. The choice of a constant zero-order rate contradicts the β·X term being proportional to cell mass.

bioprocess-018.question: The specific growth rate of a microorganism with substrate inhibition is given by μ = μmax·S/(Ks + S + S²/Ki). With Ks = 0.20 g/L and Ki = 5.0 g/L, at what substrate concentration S is μ at its maximum?
bioprocess-018.explanation: Differentiating μ with respect to S and setting it to zero gives Ks − S²/Ki = 0, so μ is at its maximum at S = √(Ks·Ki) = √(0.20 × 5.0) = 1.0 g/L. There, μ = μmax × 1.0 ÷ (0.20 + 1.0 + 0.20) ≈ 0.71μmax. 2.6 g/L is the arithmetic mean of Ks and Ki, whereas the maximum lies at the geometric mean. 5.0 g/L is Ki itself; at this concentration the S²/Ki term is as large as S, and μ has already fallen to about 0.49μmax. With substrate inhibition, the substrate is not added all at once but is kept at a low concentration near the optimum, for example by fed-batch culture.

bioprocess-019.question: In the dynamic method for measuring kLa in an aerated, agitated vessel during cultivation, aeration is stopped for a while and then restarted, and the change in dissolved oxygen concentration CL is measured. What does the rate of decrease in CL while aeration is stopped represent?
choices: kLa itself: the faster CL falls, the greater the capacity to supply oxygen from bubbles to the liquid
The driving force C* − CL: the faster CL falls, the greater the driving force for oxygen transfer
The oxygen uptake rate of all the cells; combined with the rise in CL after aeration resumes, it gives kLa
bioprocess-019.explanation: When aeration is stopped, oxygen is no longer supplied from bubbles, so the dissolved oxygen balance becomes dCL/dt = −qO₂X; CL falls almost linearly, and its slope gives the oxygen uptake rate of all the cells, qO₂X. After aeration resumes, dCL/dt = kLa(C* − CL) − qO₂X, so kLa is calculated from the rising CL curve and the uptake rate found earlier. While aeration is stopped no oxygen transfer occurs, so the rate of decrease does not represent kLa, and it is wrong to say a faster fall means a greater supply capacity. C* − CL is a driving force with units of concentration, a different quantity from the rate of decrease, which has units of concentration per time. During the measurement, CL should not be allowed to fall below the critical dissolved oxygen concentration.

bioprocess-020.question: For an enzyme immobilized in a porous support, diffusion of substrate into the support is slower than the reaction. Compared with the free enzyme, how do the apparent kinetic parameters fitted to the Michaelis–Menten equation change (assume no enzyme deactivation)?
choices: Diffusion lowers only the maximum rate, so the apparent Km is unchanged and the apparent Vmax becomes smaller
The substrate concentration inside the support is lower than outside, so the apparent Km rises and the rate falls at low concentrations
The substrate stays longer inside the support, so the apparent Km falls and the rate exceeds that of the free enzyme at low concentrations
bioprocess-020.explanation: Inside the support, substrate diffusing in from outside is consumed as it penetrates, so the substrate concentration inside is lower than in the outer liquid. At low substrate concentrations the rate is sensitive to concentration, so the diffusion limitation acts strongly on the low-concentration side and the apparent Km increases. At sufficiently high substrate concentrations the reaction proceeds at a nearly zero-order rate deep into the support, so the apparent Vmax does not fall much. The choice in which Km is unchanged and only Vmax falls contradicts the smaller effect of diffusion at high concentrations. The choice in which longer residence lowers Km overlooks that slow diffusion actually lowers the substrate concentration inside. Smaller support particles weaken the diffusion limitation.
